name: Aesthetic-usability effect
statement: Interfaces that look better are rated easier to use, a correlation that is large between ratings and much smaller when usability is measured by what people do.
meaning: The claim has two halves that are usually merged. The first half is a correlation between two judgements, how beautiful a screen looks and how easy it looks to use, both given by the same person on the same scale before anybody touches the system. That half is large and repeats. The second half is a causal claim, that beauty makes a system work better or makes its real problems easier to forgive. That half is what design writing takes from the research, and it rests on a smaller and less agreeable set of experiments. Kurosu and Kashimura's term for the rated quantity was apparent usability, and the word apparent was doing work.

origin.note: A two-page short paper at pages 292 and 293, which could not be obtained for this entry. Tractinsky, who worked from its materials, describes it as setting apparent usability, a rating of how easy a screen looks, against inherent usability, which was seven features of the layout rather than any measurement of use.

evidence: Kurosu and Kashimura had people rate 26 ATM screen layouts on how easy each looked to use and on how beautiful it was. Nobody operated an ATM. Their two pages could not be obtained, so everything here about that study is read off Tractinsky (1997), who used their materials and thanks Kurosu for his help. Tractinsky's Table 1 gives their aesthetics to apparent usability correlation as 0.589, and his text as 0.59. He records that the 26 layouts were solicited from 26 people: 9 GUI designers, 6 industrial engineers, 8 engineers and 3 secretaries. Those are the designers, not the raters, and his paper nowhere gives the number of Japanese raters. Tractinsky obtained the layouts from Kurosu and rebuilt them in Hebrew, swapping a bowing figure for an hourglass and the yen symbol for the Hebrew word for confirmation. Experiment 1 showed them to 104 first-year engineering students on an overhead projector for about 20 seconds each, on two scales of 1 to 10. Averaged across the 26 designs, aesthetics and apparent usability correlated at 0.921, and a test for the difference against the Japanese figure gave Z = 3.09, p = 0.001. Experiment 2 separated the two ratings into different rounds for 81 students and returned 0.832. Experiment 3 sat 108 third-year students at individual computers with the order randomised and returned 0.920. Mean ratings tracked the Japanese ones, 5.9 against 6.0 for aesthetics and 5.4 against 5.8 for apparent usability. The Israeli spread was wider. Aesthetics ran 3.5 to 8.5 against 5.2 to 6.8, and apparent usability 2.7 to 8.5 against 4.4 to 6.5. Of the seven inherent usability features, only keypad type and grouping tracked apparent usability in Israel. The Japanese associated ease of use with the horizontal keypad and the Israelis with the telephone keypad. Israelis rated designs with fewer groups as more usable, against the advice in the usability literature.

replication.headline: The rating-to-rating correlation repeats every time it is attempted; the experiments that manipulate beauty and then measure behaviour disagree with each other.
replication.detail: Tractinsky ran three experiments in Israel and reported correlations of 0.921, 0.832 and 0.920 against the Japanese 0.589, computed on 26 design means rather than on participants. He designed the study to show the opposite. His stated expectation was that Israeli correlations would be lower, because Israeli culture is described in the paper as action oriented against a Japanese aesthetic tradition, and his abstract records that the cross-cultural differences he found were not in the hypothesised direction. He also tested his own result for artefacts. Splitting the two ratings into separate rounds did not remove the correlation, and a multitrait-multimethod matrix met the discriminant-validity requirement in 5 of 12 comparisons. He notes that most failures involve Experiment 1, the design most exposed to method bias, and that comparisons drawn only from Experiments 2 and 3 meet it 3 times in 4. Tractinsky, Katz and Ikar then had 132 third-year students use an ATM simulation, 124 of them analysed after 8 exclusions, crossing three levels of aesthetics with two levels of real usability. Perceived aesthetics and perceived usability correlated at 0.66 before use and 0.71 after. The usability manipulation worked, raising mean task time from 23.5 to 37.5 seconds, F(1, 118) = 414.05, p < 0.001. The aesthetics manipulation moved post-use perceived usability, F(2, 117) = 4.75, p < 0.01, and post-use perceived aesthetics, F(2, 117) = 9.73, p < 0.001, with a stepdown F(2, 116) = 4.49, p < 0.01. Every test of the usability factor on post-use perception came back below significance. Aesthetics changed no behaviour at all: F(2, 118) = 0.01, p = 0.987 on completion times, and no effect on the 1.26 errors people made on average. Tuch and colleagues ran the same crossing on four versions of an online shop with 80 participants. They found no effect of aesthetics on perceived usability before use, F(1, 76) = 0.582, p = 0.448, partial eta-squared 0.008, none after use, and an effect running the other way, from real usability to post-use ratings of beauty. Sonderegger and Sauer are the clearest case for the performance claim. Sixty Swiss pupils used one of two mobile phone simulations, and the appealing one drew higher usability ratings, 6.14 against 5.32 on a single item, F(1, 57) = 9.8, p < 0.01, and 6.13 against 5.19 on the PSSUQ, F(1, 57) = 20.8, p < 0.001. It also produced faster work, 147.7 seconds against 198.5, F(1, 57) = 8.9, p < 0.01, fewer errors, 2.0 against 4.8, F(1, 57) = 12.0, p < 0.001, and better interaction efficiency, 59 per cent against 46. The same laboratory's earlier study points the other way. Sauer and Sonderegger gave 60 adults a mobile phone at three levels of prototype fidelity and found no main effect of aesthetics on completion time, F(1, 36) = 2.31, p > 0.05, and none on interaction efficiency, F(1, 36) = 2.51, p > 0.05. Two meta-analyses by overlapping author teams bracket the size of the performance effect. Thielsch, Scharfen, Masoudi and Reuter pooled 25 studies, 101 effects and 3,025 participants at g = 0.12, with high heterogeneity and no significant moderator. Schlamann, Nestler and Thielsch pooled 31 studies, 234 effect sizes and 18,794 participants at g = 0.29, again with high unexplained heterogeneity.

study.cite: Tractinsky, N. (1997). Aesthetics and apparent usability: empirically assessing cultural and methodological issues. CHI '97, 115-122.

limits: The correlation is between two ratings collected minutes apart from one person, and in the two founding studies it is computed across 26 design means, not across people. On performance the literature splits, and the split survives pooling. The 2026 meta-analysis puts the pooled estimate at g = 0.29. Its own deposited analysis script records the interval and the spread behind it. The headline model returns g = 0.2933, 95% CI 0.0766 to 0.5101, p = 0.0097, with a 95% prediction interval for the true effect of -1.0739 to 1.6606. Those three figures were read off the authors' R script on Zenodo, not off the article, which could not be opened. Its abstract also names a-posteriori-defined aesthetic conditions as a control variable suggesting that prior user experience confounds the estimate. Tractinsky, Katz and Ikar's own usability manipulation shows how thin the behavioural ground is: of the 14-second gap their manipulation produced, 9 seconds were deliberate system delays written into the program. Two documents behind this entry could not be opened on 21 September 2026. Unpaywall, OpenAlex and Semantic Scholar all record the Kurosu and Kashimura paper as gold open access, and all give the ACM PDF as its only location. Every route to it returned Cloudflare's interstitial challenge rather than a paywall or a price. The CHI '95 electronic proceedings copy at prior.sigchi.org returned 503, and the Internet Archive is blocked by this session's egress, so neither was a test of the document. Hassenzahl's 2004 study, which reports pre-use correlations of 0.07 and 0.14 once hedonic quality is controlled, is described here only from Tuch and colleagues' Table 1, and its own text was not read. Crossref, OpenAlex, Unpaywall and Semantic Scholar all record it as closed, and the copies on Academia.edu and ResearchGate require accounts. The meta-analysis is published under CC-BY 4.0 and Taylor and Francis answered every route with the same bot challenge, which is not a paywall and may not stop the next reader. Searches covered Crossref, DataCite, OpenAlex, Semantic Scholar, Unpaywall, PubMed, CORE, OpenAIRE, Zenodo, the Swiss Open Access Repository, the authors' own university pages and general web search.
misreadings: The most common error is arithmetic. A figure of 0.92 invites the reader to picture 104 people, and it describes 26 pictures of an ATM whose ratings were averaged first. Correlations across design means are larger than correlations across individuals, and neither founding paper reports how consistent any single person was. The second error is about what was measured. Inherent usability in Kurosu and Kashimura meant seven properties of a layout, such as where the keypad sits and how the keys are grouped, and in Tractinsky's three experiments no participant completed a task. The third concerns Tractinsky himself. He is quoted as confirming the effect, and he ran the study hoping to break it, predicting weaker correlations in Israel and finding stronger ones. That is a stronger result than a confirmation, and it is also the point at which the paper stops explaining anything: his discussion offers three competing accounts of why Israelis correlated more, including the wider spread of their own ratings. The fourth is that original authors misreport themselves. Sonderegger and Sauer describe their own earlier study as finding that users took more time with the more appealing mobile phone. That paper reports no significant main effect of aesthetics on completion time, F(1, 36) = 2.31, p > 0.05. What it found was a cross-over interaction with prototype fidelity, F(1, 36) = 6.59, p < 0.05. The appealing design was slowest as a computer prototype, at 342.1 seconds, and fastest as a working handset, at 138.4. Published abstracts drift from their own methods sections too. The abstract of Sonderegger and Sauer, on PubMed and on the deposited article alike, gives 60 adolescents aged 14 to 17; the method section of the same article gives ages 13 to 16 with a mean of 14.2. The Nielsen Norman Group article that carries the effect to most designers states that Kurosu and Kashimura tested 252 participants. That figure could not be checked against the paper, which was not obtainable, and it is not in Tractinsky's account of their study either.
